summary: This informational document describes the Argon2 memory-hard function for password hashing and proof-of-work, with an implementer-oriented description and test vectors. It is a product of the CFRG in the IRTF and aims to simplify adoption of Argon2 in Internet protocols.

plainLanguage.summary:
Argon2 turns a password into a value that is expensive to compute and impossible to work backwards from. It does this by using a lot of memory, not just a lot of processor time.

That matters because a thief with a list of stolen hashes can try guesses in parallel on cheap hardware. If each guess needs a megabyte of memory, the attack gets much harder to run in bulk.

questions: what is the difference between argon2id argon2i and argon2d
subtitle: A password hashing function that is deliberately hungry for memory, so attackers cannot cheaply guess at scale.

tldr.problem: A stolen list of password hashes is only useful to a thief if guessing is cheap. Hash functions made for general use can be run far faster on special hardware than on the servers that check them.
tldr.mechanism: Argon2 fills a large block of memory using a BLAKE2b-based compression function and then makes further passes over it, so each guess costs memory as well as time. It comes in three variants, one of which must be supported.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives the algorithm, the parameters to use and test vectors. Argon2id MUST be supported, and two settings are named as the first and second recommended choices.

facts.label: First recommended option
facts.value: Argon2id, t=1, p=4, 2 GiB of RAM, 128-bit salt, 256-bit tag

facts.label: Second recommended option
facts.value: Argon2id, t=3, p=4, 64 MiB of RAM, 128-bit salt, 256-bit tag

today: RFC 9106 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is the Crypto Forum Research Group's consensus description of Argon2 version 1.3, written so that implementations can agree on the same output. The RFC requires support for Argon2id and names two default parameter sets, one for general use and one for memory-constrained environments.

sections.title: What Argon2 Is For
sections.content:
The RFC describes Argon2, a memory-hard function for password hashing and proof-of-work applications, with an implementer-oriented description and test vectors. Its stated purpose is to simplify the adoption of Argon2 in Internet protocols. It corresponds to version 1.3 of the Argon2 hash function, and it represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

Memory-hard means the function is designed to be expensive in memory as well as in time. Argon2 is a streamlined design that aims at the highest memory-filling rate and effective use of several computing units while still defending against trade-off attacks, where an attacker tries to get the same result with less memory by doing more work. It is optimised for the x86 architecture and exploits the cache and memory organisation of recent Intel and AMD processors.

There are three variants. Argon2d uses data-dependent memory access, which suits cryptocurrencies and proof-of-work applications where side-channel timing attacks are not a threat. Argon2i uses data-independent memory access, which is preferred for password hashing and password-based key derivation, and makes more passes over the memory to protect against trade-off attacks. Argon2id works as Argon2i for the first half of the first pass over the memory and as Argon2d for the rest, giving both side-channel protection and the brute-force cost savings of time-memory trade-offs. Argon2id MUST be supported by any implementation of this document; Argon2d and Argon2i MAY be supported.

Argon2 is also a mode of operation over a fixed-input-length compression function G and a variable-input-length hash function H. The function H could in principle be anything that produces up to 64 bytes of output, but this document uses BLAKE2b.
sections.plainLanguage:
Argon2 is a way of turning a password into a stored value that cannot be reversed, and that costs a lot of memory to compute.

There are three versions of it. One is designed for systems where nobody can watch the timing, one for password storage, and one that mixes both approaches and is the one every implementation has to support.

sections.title: The Inputs and the Output
sections.content:
Argon2 takes a set of parameters and produces a tag.

The message P is the password for password hashing applications, and must be no longer than 2^32 - 1 bytes. The nonce S is the salt; it must be no longer than 2^32 - 1 bytes, 16 bytes is recommended for password hashing, and the salt should be unique for each password. The degree of parallelism p sets how many independent but synchronising chains, called lanes, can run, and must be an integer from 1 to 2^24 - 1. The tag length T must be a whole number of bytes from 4 to 2^32 - 1. The memory size m must be a whole number of kibibytes from 8p to 2^32 - 1; the real number of blocks is m', which is m rounded down to the nearest multiple of 4p. The number of passes t tunes the running time independently of the memory size and must be an integer from 1 to 2^32 - 1. The version number v must be the single byte 0x13. A secret K and associated data X are both optional and each must be no longer than 2^32 - 1 bytes. The type y selects the variant: 0 for Argon2d, 1 for Argon2i and 2 for Argon2id.

The output is the tag, a string of T bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller chooses the password, a salt, how much memory to use, how many lanes to use, how many passes to make and how long a result should be. The result is a tag of the requested length.

sections.title: How Argon2 Fills Its Memory
sections.content:
Argon2 uses an internal compression function G with two 1024-byte inputs, a 1024-byte output, and an internal hash function H whose output length is given as an exponent. That function is BLAKE2b, called with the data padded to a multiple of 128 bytes. A variable-length hash function H' is built on top of it.

The operation has eight steps.

First, a 64-byte value H_0 is computed from all the parameters and inputs, each prefixed by its length; a value of zero length is simply absent, but its length field stays. Second, the memory is allocated as m' blocks of 1024 bytes, where m' = 4 * p * floor(m / 4p), and arranged as a matrix B[i][j] with p rows, the lanes, and q = m'/p columns. Third, the first block of each lane is computed. Fourth, the second block of each lane is computed. Fifth, the remaining blocks are computed as B[i][j] = G(B[i][j-1], B[l][z]), and the computation must proceed slice by slice: all blocks of slice 0 for all lanes, then slice 1, and so on.

Sixth, if there is more than one pass, the computation repeats, but each new block is exclusive-ored with the old value. Seventh, after the last pass the final block C is the exclusive-or of the last column of every lane. Eighth, the tag is H'^T(C).

To allow blocks to be computed in parallel, the matrix is divided into four vertical slices. The intersection of a slice and a lane is a segment of length q/4, and segments of the same slice can be computed in parallel because they do not reference each other.

Which block is referenced is decided by two 32-bit values. In Argon2d they are simply the first and second 32-bit words of the previous block. In Argon2i they are computed from a value Z built from the pass number, lane number, slice number, total blocks, total passes and type, so that the choice does not depend on the data. Argon2id uses the Argon2i method for pass 0 in slices 0 and 1 and the Argon2d method otherwise. The lane is l = J_2 mod p, and a non-uniform mapping turns J_1 into the index z of the reference block.

The compression function G takes two 1024-byte blocks, exclusive-ors them, and treats the result as an 8 by 8 matrix of 16-byte registers. The BLAKE2b-based permutation P is applied to each row and then to each column, and G outputs the result exclusive-ored with the original. The permutation P is the BLAKE2b round function over a 4 by 4 matrix of 64-bit words, except that the additions include a 64-bit multiplication. That multiplication is the only difference from BLAKE2b, and it is there to increase the circuit depth and the running time of application-specific integrated circuit implementations, while keeping roughly the same running time on processors thanks to parallelism and pipelining.
sections.plainLanguage:
Argon2 fills its memory with blocks of data, each one computed from the previous block and one taken from elsewhere in the memory. Each pass over the memory mixes everything again, so the final result depends on the whole buffer.

That is what makes it costly: you cannot skip most of the memory and still get the same answer.

sections.title: Choosing the Parameters
sections.content:
Argon2d suits settings where the adversary has no regular access to the system's memory or processor, so cannot run timing-based side-channel attacks or recover the password faster using garbage collection. These are typical of back-end servers and cryptocurrency mining. For cryptocurrency mining that takes 0.1 seconds on a 2 GHz processor using one core, the suggestion is Argon2d with 2 lanes and 250 MB of RAM.

Argon2id suits more realistic settings, where the adversary may be on the same machine, use its processor or mount cold-boot attacks. Three examples are given: back-end server authentication taking 0.5 seconds on a 2 GHz processor with 4 cores, using Argon2id with 8 lanes and 4 GiB of RAM; key derivation for hard-drive encryption taking 3 seconds on a 2 GHz processor with 2 cores, using Argon2id with 4 lanes and 6 GiB of RAM; and front-end server authentication taking 0.5 seconds on a 2 GHz processor with 2 cores, using Argon2id with 4 lanes and 1 GiB of RAM.

For general use the RFC gives a procedure. If a uniformly safe option that is not tailored to the application or hardware is acceptable, choose Argon2id with one iteration, 4 lanes, m = 2^21 (2 GiB of RAM), a 128-bit salt and a 256-bit tag. This is the first recommended option. If much less memory is available, the uniformly safe option is Argon2id with three iterations, 4 lanes, m = 2^16 (64 MiB of RAM), a 128-bit salt and a 256-bit tag. This is the second recommended option.

Otherwise, pick the type, choosing Argon2id if the difference between the types is not clear or side-channel attacks are a real threat. Use 4 lanes. Work out the most memory each call can afford and turn that into m, and the most time each call can afford. Choose a salt length of 128 bits, which is enough for every application but can be cut to 64 bits when space is tight. Choose a tag length of 128 bits, enough for most applications including key derivation, and longer if longer keys are needed. If side-channel attacks are a real threat or the choice is uncertain, turn on the memory-wiping option in the library call. Then run with different numbers of passes and find the largest t that stays inside the time budget; if even one pass exceeds it, reduce the memory. Use the values found.
sections.plainLanguage:
How much memory and how much time an attacker gets depends on the settings. The RFC gives two ready-made answers and a step-by-step method for anything else.

The safe default uses two gigabytes of memory. A lighter option uses sixty-four megabytes.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives test vectors for all three variants, each with the complete output tag and, for convenience, some interim values: the first and last memory block of each pass, and the pre-hashing digest. The vectors use a 32-byte password, a 16-byte salt, an 8-byte secret, 12 bytes of associated data, 32 KiB of memory, 3 passes, 4 lanes and a 32-byte tag.

These vectors exist so that two implementations of Argon2 can be checked against each other. If they produce the same tag for the same inputs and parameters, they agree.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes known-answer tests for each variant. An implementation can run them and check that it produces the same tag, which is how two independent implementations are shown to agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As a hash function, Argon2's collision and preimage resistance match those of BLAKE2b: producing a collision takes 2^256 inputs, and finding a preimage takes 2^512 attempts. Its key derivation security is set by the key length and the size of the internal state of H'. A minimum of (2^128, 2^length(K)) calls to BLAKE2b are needed to tell the output of a keyed Argon2 from random.

Trade-off attacks compute a memory-hard function while storing fewer blocks, at the cost of more calls to the internal compression function. The advantage is measured by the reduction factor applied to the time-area product. The best-known attack on one-pass and two-pass Argon2i is a low-storage attack that reduces the time-area product by a factor of 5. For Argon2i with three or more passes the reduction factor depends on memory size and pass count: 3 for 3 passes, 2.5 for 4 passes and 2 for 6 passes at one gibibyte of memory, growing by about 0.5 with every doubling of the memory. To prevent trade-off attacks completely, the number of passes must exceed the binary logarithm of memory minus 26. The best attack on one-pass Argon2i is asymptotically bounded by O(m^0.233) in the number of blocks m, which is also the best any attack could achieve. The best trade-off attack on t-pass Argon2d is the ranking trade-off attack, reducing the time-area product by a factor of 1.33. For Argon2id, the best attack on one pass combines the low-storage attack for the first half of the memory with the ranking attack for the second, giving a factor of about 2.1, and the best attack on t passes is the ranking attack with a factor of 1.33.

For a defender with a fixed time budget, the attack cost estimates imply that three passes is close to optimal for Argon2i at most reasonable memory sizes, while one pass maximises the attack cost for Argon2d and Argon2id.

The recommendations follow from this. Argon2id with one pass and 2 GiB of memory is the first recommended option and the default for all environments; it resists side-channel attacks and maximises adversarial cost on dedicated brute-force hardware. Argon2id with three passes and 64 MiB of memory is the second recommended option and the default for memory-constrained environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The published attacks on Argon2 all cost the attacker a factor of a few compared with the honest cost. The RFC gives the numbers, and the recommendation is simply to use Argon2id with one pass and two gigabytes unless memory is tight.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT STEPS OF THE ARGON2 OPERATION (RFC 9106)

data.title: Argon2 operation
data.code:
1. H_0 = H^(64)(LE32(p) || LE32(T) || LE32(m) || LE32(t) ||
        LE32(v) || LE32(y) || LE32(length(P)) || P ||
        LE32(length(S)) || S || LE32(length(K)) || K ||
        LE32(length(X)) || X)

2. m' = 4 * p * floor (m / 4p)
   Memory is a matrix B[i][j] with p lanes and q = m'/p columns.

3. B[i][0] = H'^(1024)(H_0 || LE32(0) || LE32(i))
4. B[i][1] = H'^(1024)(H_0 || LE32(1) || LE32(i))
5. B[i][j] = G(B[i][j-1], B[l][z])
6. Further passes:
   B[i][0] = G(B[i][q-1], B[l][z]) XOR B[i][0]
   B[i][j] = G(B[i][j-1], B[l][z]) XOR B[i][j]
7. C = B[0][q-1] XOR B[1][q-1] XOR ... XOR B[p-1][q-1]
8. The output tag is H'^T(C).

items.title: First recommended
items.text: Argon2id, t=1 iteration, p=4 lanes, m=2^21 (2 GiB of RAM), 128-bit salt, 256-bit tag.

items.title: Second recommended
items.text: Argon2id, t=3 iterations, p=4 lanes, m=2^16 (64 MiB of RAM), 128-bit salt, 256-bit tag.

items.title: Salt length
items.text: 128 bits is enough for every application; 64 bits if space is tight.

items.title: Tag length
items.text: 128 bits is enough for most applications, including key derivation.
